html:
Why “Good job” may be quietly killing the best in us — and what great work actually demands.

My son asked me to watch Whiplash last week. I sat down expecting a film about music. I got something else entirely a film about hunger, about the distance between good and great, and about the terrible price of comfort.

Much of the movie stayed with me. The sweat, the blood, the obsession. But one line settled into my mind like a stone dropping into still water, and it hasn’t left since.

“The two most dangerous words in the English language are: Good job.”

I turned it over and over. Was this cruelty dressed up as philosophy? Or was it the most honest thing someone had said about talent in years?

The more I sat with it, the more I knew. It was the latter.

We Did Not Grow Up on Encouragement

I grew up in a world that offered no such softness. There was no applause waiting at the end of mediocre effort. There was criticism. There was silence. There was the blunt weight of expectation, unsoftened by praise. It felt terrible most of the time.

But something happened for those of us who did not turn away. Something almost miraculous, in the way that all difficult things, when survived, become miraculous in hindsight. The resistance — the friction of being told it was not good enough became the very fuel. We fought for the standard. We earned the standard. And the standard, earned that way, became ours forever.

The ones who gave up were, perhaps, always going to give up. That is a harder truth than it sounds. Encouragement does not change what is inside a person. It only delays the revealing of it.

Today, encouragement has become the default. We celebrate the attempt before the result. We hand out rewards before expectations are even met. We are seeking relaxation before we have grown tired enough. We are reaching for reward before we have arrived anywhere worth rewarding.

And slowly, quietly — we become useless to ourselves.

The Invitation We Keep Refusing

This brings me to a poem I have returned to many times over the years. It was written by Oriah Mountain Dreamer, and it asks — with tremendous gentleness and tremendous demand — the only questions that actually matter.

Oriah Mountain Dreamer — The Invitation

It doesn’t interest me what you do for a living. I want to know what you ache for and if you dare to dream of meeting your heart’s longing.

It doesn’t interest me how old you are. I want to know if you will risk looking like a fool for love, for your dream, for the adventure of being alive.

I want to know if you can sit with pain, mine or your own, without moving to hide it, or fade it, or fix it.

I want to know if you can live with failure, yours and mine, and still stand at the edge of the lake and shout to the silver of the full moon, “Yes.”

I want to know if you can get up after the night of grief and despair, weary and bruised to the bone, and do what needs to be done to feed the children.

I want to know if you will stand in the centre of the fire with me and not shrink back.

I want to know what sustains you from the inside when all else falls away.

I want to know if you can be alone with yourself and if you truly like the company you keep in the empty moments.

Read it again. Notice what she does not ask. She does not ask about your credentials, your titles, your accolades, how many people clapped for you. She asks if you can bear the weight of being alive — the weight of longing, of failure, of sorrow, of the fire.

That is not an encouragement. That is an invitation into something far older and harder and more true.

We are entering an age that will not be soft. The world is becoming more ruthless, not less. The polished surface of nicety is wearing thin. What lies beneath — in every professional arena, in every creative endeavour, in every life — is something that can only be discovered through difficulty.

So perhaps it is time. Time to retrain the mind. Time to stop treating hardness as an obstacle and start treating it as the path. Time to understand that everything worth having in this life will be — must be — hard-earned.

Not because suffering is noble for its own sake. But because the version of yourself that comes through the fire is the only version capable of standing at the edge of the lake and shouting, freely and without doubt, “Yes.”

— Sakti Bagchi
